title: How would you estimate the size of the US dog food market?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How big is the US market for dog food each year?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: Pet markets are popular in interviews because the chain of assumptions is clear: homes, dog owners, dogs per home, spend per dog. Have a go at your own estimate before reading on.
body:
The question

How big is the US market for dog food each year?

The approach

Households × share with dogs × dogs per household × spend per dog.

Tip: If you are unsure of a number, say your assumption and why. A reasoned guess beats a confident invention.

Step by step

  1. US households: 130M
  2. × 38% own a dog
  3. × 1.5 dogs per dog-owning household
  4. × $500 food spend per dog per year

That gives about $37.1B a year.

Does it make sense?

About $40 a month per dog, which is in line with a mid-priced bag of dry food.

Separate dogs, food types and channels

A £37 billion-style estimate for a market measured in dollars is only a starting point because spend differs sharply by pet size and food choice. Small dogs consume less by weight; premium wet food and special diets can cost much more per serving than basic dry food.

Try a two-segment check. Suppose 70% of dogs spend $400 a year on food and 30% spend $800. Weighted average spend is $520 per dog. Using the original estimated dog population of about 74 million, the market is then approximately $38.5 billion. The output is close to the original estimate, but now you know what drives the spending assumption.

Clarify whether treats, supplements and veterinary diets count, and distinguish the retail value of food sold from manufacturers' net sales. A case about a pet-food producer needs the latter, not simply the value at checkout.
